<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Stephen F. Lynch, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Cleo Fields>: We strongly support community banks and credit unions and stand ready to work with Republicans to advance sensible reforms to do just that. However, this package of overwhelmingly Republican and partisan bills represents the greatest amount of bank deregulation since before the 2008 global financial crisis. Instead of focusing on sensible improvements to support community banks and credit unions on Main Street, this bill will help megabanks on Wall Street and harm consumers. It undermines consumer protection, community reinvestment, and anti-discrimination safeguards, as well as impairs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's (CFPB) ability to issue any new rules. It also includes reforms that will chill international regulatory cooperation, as well as fuel faster industry consolidation by effectively exempting most bank mergers from review. In other words, this legislation does not provide access to capital for Main Street.
This bill's partisan approach is a departure from recent action the House took to support community financial institutions. Specifically, Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats recently worked with Chairman French Hill and Committee Republicans to include 12 provisions to help community financial institution in H.R. 6644, the ``Housing for the 21st Century Act.'' Five of those provisions were led by Committee Democrats, with four others co-led by Committee Democrats. In February 2026, the House passed that package overwhelmingly by a vote of 390 to 9.
POISON PILLS UNDERMINING SENSIBLE RELIEF FOR COMMUNITY FINANCIAL
INSTITUTIONS
This bill falls well short of what we know can be done on a bipartisan basis to promote, preserve, and enhance access to banking services for Main Street communities. H.R. 6955 consists of 30 Republican bills and only a few Democratic bills. Unlike our package of community bank reforms included in the housing bill, fully nine of the provisions in this package are poison pills and opposed by all Democratic members of this committee, and another seven provisions were opposed by most. Below are the nine provisions opposed by all Committee Democratic Members that were included in the package:
• Sec. 201: H.R. 3380--the ``Taking Account of
Institutions with Low Operation Risk (TAILOR) Act''
(Loudermilk), (5/21/25 markup, 29-23). This section
contains sweeping and harmful partisan reforms that
would require banking regulators and the CFPB to tailor
all regulations for all their regulated entities, not
just community banks, to account for a wide variety of
risk profiles and industry costs (but not benefits).
Given this bill requires any new rule to be tailored
not just to types of institutions but individual
institutions, any one of thousands of banks, credit
unions, or nonbank financial companies would have a
basis to sue and block any new rule from being
implemented. The ANS eliminated a lookback provision
but would still require any new rule to follow this new
procedure. This section would significantly impair the
CFPB and the banking regulators' ability to issue or
update any rules, including those that apply to the
largest financial companies that community banks and
credit unions compete with.
• Sec. 202: H.R. 2835--the ``Small Bank
Holding Company Relief Act'' (Donalds), (6/10/25
markup, 30 20). This section would double the
consolidated asset threshold from $3 billion to $6
billion for bank holding companies (BHCs) and savings
and loan holding companies (SLHCs) to be eligible for
the Federal Reserve's Small Bank Holding Company and
Savings and Loan Holding Company Policy Statement. This
statement exempts small BHCs and SLHCs from
consolidated risk-based capital and leverage
requirements, reduces reporting requirements, expedites
bank mergers, and allows them to have higher debt
flexibility to finance bank acquisitions. This policy
was first implemented by the Fed in 1980 to help the
smallest banks with less than $150 million in assets,
and Congress has subsequently increased this threshold
three times, last in 2018, to $3 billion today. While
the ANS reduces the proposed threshold from $25 billion
to $6 billion, this is still a sizable increase and
much higher than an inflation-based increase to $4
billion. This also ignores other sweeping rollbacks for
capital requirements for these same banks provided in
other sections of the bill, like the next one.
• Sec. 301: H.R. 3379--the ``Halting Uncertain
Methods and Practices in Supervision (HUMPS) Act''
(Fitzgerald), (5/21/25 markup, 29-23). This section
would significantly rollback oversight of bank
management by requiring the banking regulators, through
the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council
(FFIEC), to develop recommendations and modify their
implementation of the CAMELS ratings framework, where
depository institutions are given composite and
component exam ratings for Capital adequacy, Asset
quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, and
Sensitivity to market risk (CAMELS). In doing so,
regulators would be required to either eliminate the
management component or significantly limit its use.
The bill also eliminates the consideration of
management with respect to certain provisions of the
Bank Holding Company Act, including with respect to
acquiring other banks and expanding the bank's
financial activities. This will significantly diminish
the ability to hold bank management, like Silicon
Valley Bank (SVB) following their failure or Wells
Fargo after their repeated violations resulting in
consumer harm, accountable for their actions.
• Sec. 401: H.R. 3446--the ``FDIC Board
Accountability Act'' (Huizenga), (7/23/25 markup, 26-
23). This section represents an attack on Biden's
appointed regulators and mandates the appointment of a
member with experience in small depository
institutions, and limits board members' terms to twelve
years. Originally, this section would also remove the
CFPB Director as a voting member of the FDIC board,
though that was removed in the ANS. Nonetheless, this
section does nothing to prevent Trump's attacks on the
independence of the FDIC or require the President to
fill the vacant FDIC Board member positions with
Democratic nominees.
• Sec. 402: H.R. 4460--the ``Stop Agency Fiat
Enforcement of Guidance (SAFE Guidance) Act'' (Meuser),
(7/23/25 markup, 26-23). The bill requires the head of
Federal financial departments and agencies--
specifically Treasury, HUD, Federal Reserve, FDIC, OCC,
NCUA, SEC, CFPB, and FHFA--to provide a so-called
``guidance clarity statement'' on a wide variety of
agency statements stipulating that they don't have a
binding effect. This would require endless numbers of
disclaimers that could chill agency communications and
hinder guidance that could be helpful for industry
participants to understand their legal obligations.
Moreover, this bill would not apply to President Trump,
who issues chaotic and contradictory policy statements
on social media, who has seized control over the
rulemaking process for these agencies. The bill also
does not overturn the action of Trump's CFPB to rescind
nearly 70 guidance documents that could help regulated
entities understand their legal obligations.
• Sec. 403: H.R. 6544--the ``Regulatory
Efficiency, Verification, Itemization, and Enhanced
Workflow (REVIEW) Act'' (Timmons), (12/17/25 markup,
30-23). This section would amend the Economic Growth
and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act of 1996 (EGRPRA)
to increase the frequency of a comprehensive regulatory
review conducted every 10 years by Federal banking
regulators to every 8 years (previously 7 years before
it was changed in the ANS) and require them to conduct
a further review of the cumulative impact of their
regulations with additional cost-benefit analysis that
ignores certain benefits, like consumer protection. The
EGRPRA process is already an elaborate one, with
extensive stakeholder engagement that typically last
three years. Moreover, with the combination of Section
302, this section arguably includes the CFPB to do this
comprehensive lookback too, despite the fact they
already do a 5-year lookback review on its regulations,
among other requirements that banking regulators are
not subject to. Furthermore, regulators already have
authority to update rules whenever it may be
appropriate, and doing an exhaustive regulatory review
every 8 years would distract regulators, including the
CFPB, from their day-to-day duties to oversee the
banking system and protect consumers.
• Sec. 404: H.R. 6550--the ``American
Financial Institution Regulatory Sovereignty and
Transparency (American FIRST) Act'' (Loudermilk), (12/
17/25 markup, 29-23). This section requires the Fed,
OCC, FDIC, and NCUA to include unusually extensive
information about their interactions with global
financial regulatory or supervisory forums, like the
Basel Committee or the Network for Greening the
Financial System, undermining and chilling such
engagement by U.S. regulators and addressing risks,
like climate-related financial risk. While certain
reporting requirements were simplified through the ANS,
the requirements are still robust and would likely
chill efforts for U.S. regulators to coordinate with
foreign regulators through these forums. This section
also ignores the many ways U.S. regulators already keep
Congress informed of such engagements and advance our
national interests with their foreign counterparts to
shape global financial regulatory policy. Committee
Republicans passed a similar bill last Congress (H.R.
4823, 118th) on a party-line vote.
• Sec. 601: H.R. 5262--the ``Bank Competition
Modernization Act'' (Fitzgerald), (9/16/25 markup, 28-
24). The section amends several banking laws to
completely waive a review for mergers that would result
in a bank under $10 billion in assets related to
competition, regardless of whether the bank would
become the only lender in a community. The section also
includes an annual adjustment calculation based on
nominal GDP, which would quickly increase the threshold
as opposed to a more typical inflation-based
adjustment. These sweeping reforms will accelerate
consolidation and lead to fewer community banks.
• Sec. 604: H.R. 1900--the ``Bank Failure
Prevention Act'' (Barr), (5/21/25 markup, 29-21). This
section would modify the bank merger review process by
limiting the Fed's ability to consider feedback from
affected stakeholders on proposed mergers. It would
also force the Fed, FDIC, and OCC to either approve or
deny a merger application within 120 days (previously
90 days before it was changed in the ANS) of receiving
an initial application, even if the application is not
complete and the merging parties have not provided all
the information regulators request to adequately assess
the merger application. These reforms will bring less
scrutiny to a rubber-stamping process that has wiped
out community banks and significantly increased the
market share of the largest banks. Previously, this
section was section 103 in the introduced version of
the bill before it was moved here.
FORGOTTEN LESSONS FROM PAST FINANCIAL CRISES
In the nearly two decades since the 2008 global crisis, we've learned a great deal about how to maintain a resilient financial system in the face of many obstacles, including through the pandemic. But this partisan package ignores those lessons and will plant the seeds for the next crisis. Moreover, while the nation grapples with an affordability crisis and surge in financial scams and fraud, costing consumers tens of billions of dollars, this package would hamper the CFPB's ability to issue any new rules, undercutting the very agency Congress established to combat financial abuses and empower consumers to protect their finances. At a time when the Trump Administration has largely shut down the CFPB and this Committee has failed to fulfill our statutory duty to have Acting Director Russell Vought testify, the last thing Congress should be doing is undermining the CFPB any further.
